extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. These questions are generated in unprompted and unconstrained settings, often querying for complex, non-factoid information, and requiring difficult entailment-like inference to solve. The dataset is designed to test models' ability to make such inferences.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1, 2019.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words (did, do, does, is, are, was, were, have, has, can, could, will, would) and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. These question/article pairs are then given to a human annotator for further processing.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as “not answerable” if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by checking if the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and if they are of sufficient length. Questions are filtered to only include those where a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five search results. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used, and each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity and keep input small.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: 1) Decide if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page. 2) For good questions, find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, or mark as 'not answerable'. 3) Mark whether the question’s answer is 'yes' or 'no'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement, resulting in 'gold-standard' labels. The original answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to these gold-standard labels. Disagreements were due to ambiguous/debatable cases or annotator errors.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Singly-annotated examples are used in the training/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset has a class imbalance with 'Yes' answers being slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). There is a correlation between the nature of the question (topic or type) and the likelihood of a 'yes' answer, though this correlation is too weak to outperform the majority baseline.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Factoid questions that ask about simple properties of entities are rare. Both the passages and questions rarely include negation, meaning detecting a 'no' answer often requires understanding that a positive assertion in the text excludes or makes unlikely a positive assertion in the question. The dataset has been updated since the analysis in the paper was carried out, so the analysis might be slightly out-of-date.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning of models for natural language understanding, specifically for answering naturally occurring yes/no questions and testing inferential abilities. It is suitable for constructing highly inferential reading comprehension datasets directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions.
